This was an exact replacement fit for my refrigerator. After I replaced this unit I found out that this was not my problem. I placed my old filter cartridge back in and it leaked the same as before. As I looked carefully at the old cartridge in the sunlight I noticed a very fine crack at one of the ports that extended under the o-ring. The new cartridge ports looked thicker. The new replacement cartridge did not leak. The water and ice will work without a cartridge in place if you want. You just won't have filtered water and ice. When you pull your old cartridge out the housing has a bypass and seals off so no water will come out of the housing when removing the cartridge (or very little water as long as it's working properly).

The water dispenser on my 5-year-old Whirlpool Gold refrigerator suddenly began having problems one day. The water slowed to a trickle. At first I thought it might be the filter, which was due to be changed, but after swapping in a new filter, the problem was worse. I was getting no flow at all. After watching a few YouTube videos, I thought the issue might be a frozen water line. I opened the freezer door for awhile (I put heavy cardboard over the opening to keep the contents as cold as possible) to allow the line to defrost, if that was, in fact, the problem. That yielded no results. I also verified that the ice maker was not making ice. I then reached out to Whirlpool - they were very responsive over Twitter, and even gave me a call, but they seemed totally clueless with little to offer other than reading canned text from a customer service rep manual (clearly those I was dealing with had little or no plumbing experience). More research led me to conclude that it might be the water filter housing. It was a bit of a gamble as I wasn't certain I'd be able to return this, but if it worked, it would save me from paying $250+ for a repair guy. I decided to go for it, and I'm glad I did. Replacing the water filter housing completely solved the problem.

The old filter housing worked with the old model filters but would not work with the newer replacement model filters. Discovered after extensive troubleshooting that the old filter housing and the new replacement filters do not properly fit together. The new filters will not fully engage the needle/pin valves in the back of the older filter housing even though the filter fully inserts and locks into place. I ordered this newer filter housing and it fixed the problem. The newer filters fit much better into this newer filter housing. The OEM's make no mention of this and they state that the the newer/latest model filters are direct replacements. I discovered this is not true.  If you are having filter issues I would recommend replacing the filter housing as there may be an issue with proper fit. I recently had the the entire roof replaced on my 25' travel trailer. Both vents had MaxAir covers on them - including the original fantastic fan vent in the rear bath. That fan had numerous cracks in the plastic flange and housing (perhaps due to an improper installation of the original vent cover) and had to be replaced. The repair shop doing the roof replacement did not replace the vent cover on the fantastic fan, telling me that "these don't work."

I made plans to add the newer model Max Air fan cover (even though I was hesitant to put a cover designed to mount to metal flange on a plastic flange)... then I found the links to this particular model. While I don't like the fact that mounting required cutting lap sealant, mounting into the roof and re-sealing the screw holes (Remember I just replaced the entire roof due to leaks that couldn't be fixed)... Once this was mounted and in place, I went inside and turned the fan on "high"... and had more air movement in the bath than I've had since this camper was new in 2004! It's perfect - and worth every penny more than the other models would have cost.

While looking for a vent cover for my Fan-Tastic kitchen vent, I found this one to be quite pricy but thought, "it must be worth it because it is made by the same manufacturer as the vent that it will be covering." Well I read through the reviews and found one that stated that it wouldn't allow the vent to open fully. I figured that maybe they didn't install it properly or something to that nature. As it turns out, they were correct! It stops the vent from opening about 2 inches shy of wide open. I guess that the only good thing that that same person did not know is that the motor that opens and closes the vent lid is not setup to operate on a set of limit switches. It in fact opens and closes until it reaches its limit of travel and then the motor will "amp out" and shut off. Because of this, you don't have to worry about damaging anything and it will work just fine. There may be some nay sayers out there that believe that the lid must open all of the way to achieve full flow through the opening but if you do the math and measure the surface area of the screen in front of the fan blades and then the surface area of the opening with the cover installed, you still will have more than enough for the fan to achieve full flow. It has not yet rained sense the install of the cover so I can't comment on how well it works in that scenario, but I will be sure to update my review as soon as it does.

This vent hood is about one and one half inches taller that our previous MaxxAir hood. This means that the cover of our Fantastic Fan will now open fully for better air flow. It’s also translucent white not heavy smoke tint so more light comes through. The mounting system is the typical four clamps screwed into the roof, two on each side.

Sadly, for a hood that is this expensive, there is NO BUG SCREEN INCLUDED. There is a grill styled opening, but no bug screen. Our original MaxxAir hood included a bug screen. (No, the old screen was not “adaptable”!) The easiest and least expensive solution is installing some fiberglass bug screen material on the inside of the grate using the same tube of roof caulk you will need to caulk over the mounting screws. Caution: be sure to use caulk designed for your roof material. Cut the material to fit inside with a one inch overlap on each side. I used a 10” by 19” sized piece. Lay a bead of caulk along the inside edge of the grate and press the screen material into the caulk bead. See the attached photo. Save a little in the tube of caulk for your mounting screws piece of the install.

I received the replacement ("Jason" branded) coupling in good order - the shipping/delivery time was less than a week. Upon receipt of this new part, I removed the original (failed) one from the washer motor and transmission shafts, and installed the replacement. It was necessary to lightly tap the coupling end-pieces onto the motor and transmission shafts using a hammer and drive socket, due to the interference fit. I would note that, in my case, the OEM coupling functioned nominally for over 25 years, which is a substantial time period. Also, the old coupling failed in the most typical manner, in which the plastic spikes were sheared off - presumably from cyclic fatigue and aging of the plastic materials.

I acknowledge that there are multiple reviews/comments here that question the quality and design/robustness of the new coupling. Therefore, I would point out that unless it's determined that the original part failed as a result of many cycles of nominal loading and aging, installing a new coupling wouldn't correct the underlying issue. If the transmission or other components in the drive train (excluding the motor itself) have developed excessive friction, this could immediately overload the coupling and cause it to fail again - even with very little use. In this case, it may be that both the original and replacement couplings failure is unrelated to this new component design.

I have used two different types of these couplings on a 110 washer, at different times. The old full plastic and this "improved" metal-ring version. This one (of which I ordered from Amazon and received an original Whirlpool part) was difficult to install because it required a lot of force to get it on the transmission spindle. I had to use a metal rod and really hammer away at it. I was concerned I might damage the transmission but I left enough room for the washer to move back as I was hammering. Getting it on the motor spindle was easy though it just required a few taps.

In the future I will seek out the full plastic version if I can find any left the next time this breaks. The reason is 1) I really don't like hammering away at the transmission or motor, and 2) the full plastic ones are machined EXACTLY to the right tolerance so you can just slide them on. Then they wear out over time... either the hole that holds the spindle wears down or one of the legs will crack and break off. According to the amazon reviews on this metal ring one it is not exactly improved, since although it prevents the hole from wearing many people report the metal ring just coming right off which isn't any better since the result is the same.

Washing machine back in service. This has metal inserts. I used a socket of the same diameter as the metal insert and a beat-up extension to gently tap into place. Just a guess, but I believe the reviewers that have a problem with insert separation might be hammering the plastic/nylon coupler instead of just the metal insert which probably would lead to premature insert separation from the couplers.

This item is made by Whirlpool, is a factory replacement part and fits my Whirlpool made Kenmore dishwasher like a glove. I was having a problem with the Jet Dry rinse aid completely emptying after only like a week or less after filling it. We run our dishwasher every day with the four of us using so many dishes and glasses. The cap was in good condition, with no cracks or other defects in it or the O-ring of the cap. The only thing I could think of was this dispenser. There would also be a small trickle of dried Jet Dry coming from the dispenser in between loads. Checking around at some of the appliance repair websites, my initial suspicion was confirmed. So I ordered this and installed it.

Looking at the rear of dispenser, a small solenoid releases both the detergent and the drying agent (I imagine at different times in the cycle). My best guess is the solenoid was not closing the valve for the Jet Dry completely. The dishwasher is about 4 1/2 years old now. I have run about 5 full loads through the dishwasher and the fill indicator has hardly moved at all, just like before my problems began, so it looks like I was right about the repair/replacement.

**Edit 8/18/13** I'm getting about a month to six weeks out of a full load of Jet Dry now, that's with using the dishwasher almost every day. This is still working great, I know now that my initial assessment was correct.

We recently bought a house with a Whirlpool Quiet Partner II (model DU1345XTVB0) dishwasher, and the rinse dispenser didn't work. It stayed filled with water and/or leaked out the rinse aid and was simply not usable.

I found this on Amazon and it appeared to be the correct part, but it's sometimes hard to tell so I was holding my breath, but it was an exact factory replacement of the existing part.

Installation was not overly complex, you have to remove the hex-drive screws from the *inside* edges of the door that hold the colored panel to the *outside* of the door, making sure not to remove the similar screws from the top of the door that hold the control panel in place. Once you remove the screws the colored panel will drop off, revealing the back side of this dispenser.

The dispenser is held in place with very small hex nuts, and I actually had to run to Lowes to get a socket driver small enough. You have to remove the screws, unhook the wire, save the protective flap of plastic (it hangs down over the dispenser to protect from wayward splashes) and metal retaining frame, remove the old dispenser, insert the new dispenser, hook up the wire, put the retaining frame in place (holding the protective flap), and reinsert the screws.

Overall it took about 20 minutes to complete. If I had to do it again it would take 5-10 minutes tops, as it is actually pretty simple once you get the layout of things.

Another issue with this dishwasher is the control panel. It uses “soft touch” switches to control various functions. Basically, these are little circles labeled “start,” “stop,” etc., on a flat plastic panel. Well, the circles crack and pop up after only a couple of years. This exposes the circuits underneath to water and other contaminants. How long should this last? I have a GE microwave with a similar panel. No problems after 20 years. STRIKE TWO.

I have worked for and with several well-known electronics companies (not appliances). The flat plastic piece with the circles is called an overlay. These could be ordered for other products for two bucks. They are held on with adhesive. Pull the old one off. Remove the backing from the new one, align, and press in place. Not Whirlpool! I even contacted the corporate offices. The overlay is not sold separately. It is part of the “Control Panel Assembly.” So, to replace the overlay you must replace all the circuits, pc boards, and wiring even if they are all still working. The cost? North of $250. Like mentioned by a few, our detergent dispenser had the little tab broken so the lid would not close. These tabs are tiny and fragile. I recommend using it gently or another replacement is in line.

Regarding the unit install: (for the Kenmore dishwasher listed above. Your mileage may vary)
Simple install. Need a T15H torx bit and remove the screws around the edge on the inside panel of the dishwasher. Once removed, the front of the dishwasher comes off. Remove the wires (brown) by gently lifting up the tabs and pull. Once the wires are disconnected, remove the metal bracket - you will see a metal bracket with 6 hex screws that you will need to remove with a 3/16 socket, then pull up the 2 plastic clips on the top/left and bottom/right of the detergent dispenser. Install is simply the reverse.

Tools to have for this job:
- T15H torx bit
- 3/16 hex socket
- flat head or your nails to lift up the 2 plastic tabs on the dispenser

First off, excellent replacement part.

My washer was throwing a tE code which indicated a thermistor failure. That is the device that checks water temperature in the machine. When I pulled the machine apart (using YouTube as my guide) I discovered that the original gasket had a small tear at its lowest part (adjacent to the drain tube). This was allowing water to seep down and corrode to contact for the thermistor. I cleaned the contacts with a small wire brush, applied some dielectric grease (can be found at Home Depot) and replace the door gasket. Problem solved.

Now, the replacement of the gasket was somewhat difficult but certain well worth the savings of having a repair person come out to fix the machine. The gasket was a perfect match. I am however disappointed with the original gasket. No idea how the tear could have occurred unless it was a defective part to begin with and slowly failed over time with use.

My washer does NOT have a drain port at the 6:00 position of the gasket, however, this item DOES. There is a hole at 6:00 hidden underneath the folds of the gasket. As a result, it does NOT work. SO, the drain port has nothing to do with the other attachments or the "port" or fenestrations also at the 6:00 position on the OEM gasket (4986ER0004). Notice, no letter at the end of the OEM product number. THE PRODUCT DESCRIPTION IS INCOMPLETE (or LG has changed the gasket and drain system since this unit was purchased in 2006). -F implies drain port. -B is for no drain port.

The good: this was a good fit for my LG WM2016CW and I was able to install by myself. The lower half of the door boot still seems to be in good condition. AFAICT, no water has leaked out.

The bad: after 1.5 years, I noticed some deformation near the top, then found a hole. I took apart the machine and found two holes (see attached pics). It looks like the rubber degraded---I see small bits of rubber near the two holes.

Notes: this includes a drain port on the bottom, but no ports on the top (what look like ports in the picture are sealed off). My original door boot never developed holes---I replaced it after 10 years after I noticed lots of bacteria/mold growth around the drain port (partly because I didn't realize how much cleaning was necessary after each wash).

Works great but the key is how long it lasts. The original element lasted 23.5 years, and a replacement I purchased from partselect.com costs twice as much and worked for only 4.5 years. This part took about 10 minutes to install and wll you need is a medium/large Philips screwdriver, a flashlight (or head light) and maybe a pair of pliers:
- turn off circuit breaker for range
- remove the 2 screws in the back plate
- gently pull element forward until attached wires stick out about 4 inches
- grab the gold colored clip at the end of each wire and gently pull to remove from element (may need pliers-I just use my hands); be sure to pull on the clips and not on the wires - if you pull a wire out of the clip you will be in deep do-do
- slide clips onto new element and push all the way on
- push element straight back so wires go through the back of the oven
- replace the two screws and turn power back on

1. Turned off circuit breaker
2. Didn’t have to pull the stove from the wall (not necessary)
3. Unscrewed element from back of oven pulled the 2 wires out.
4. Because of risk of having wires slip back into the insulation decided to use small clips to prevent that from happening.
5. There was a break on the element that was clearly visible.
6. Tried to just reach to the back to pull and unclip the wires.
7. So I had to take the door off which made the install so much easier.
8. Vacuumed and cleaned out the bottom of oven
9. Reached to the back using both hands and the install took a few minutes.
10. Turned circuit breaker back on and turned oven on and VOILA oven heats up as it should.
11. Trust your ability to do this and save yourself some time and money. As, I did at 70 plus.

Replacing the broken items in my refrigerator was not straight forward but I got it done. If you have a broken shelf clip like this, here's how I replaced mine:
1. Use a tiny drill bit and drill a hole about 1/4" deep into the round peg that will be flush on an installed clip
2. Screw a screw part way into that tiny hole drilled in step 1
3. Use a pair of pliers and pull outward on the screw to pull the round peg out. Note that it may come all the way out or it may not
4. Once you have the peg out or out as far as it will go, pull the rest of the broken clip out. If the clip remains tight to the refrigerator case, use a plastic putty knife and work it around the clip to work it out
5. Place the new clip in place and use a hammer to hammer the round peg flush with the clip.

You may end up with 2 tiny barbs broken off in the refrigerator case. Use a small nail to drive them into the case and off to the side.

I have had 3 of these elements in my Electrolux dryer in the last 6 years (including the one it came with).  The main reason I have had to replace the element is 2-fold:  (1) I was using flexible dryer duct that traveled around 20 feet before exiting the house.  As you may know, flexible duct is horrible at collecting lint in the folds and won't fully clean out even if you use a leaf-blower.  This likely sped up the process of the element overheating.  However, the other reason is (2) The design of the element allows the inner partition of the element to warp and eventually touch the outer sides of the canister, causing a ground condition and basically killing your element.  Had they designed this thing a little better, the element wouldn't warp and wouldn't cause a ground-out even if the dryer was getting a bit too hot.  Considering how much these things cost, that's a big deal.  So, to summarize, install solid ductwork (cheap and easy, so no excuses!).  Second, realize that over time, your element will warp and eventually fail unless they change the design (not likely). B-minus....

The quality of this replacement part is about the same as the part that came with the dryer: It sucks. There is no other way to put it. The center plenum has 90° lips bent on them to limit warping - but the anti-warp lip is only on the center 1/3 of the plenum. So, the hot end of the plenum twists and distorts until the heating element grounds out against the housing (bad). In my case, I had TWO elements 'self-ground' so my only heating option was 'high' as all three elements were 'on' any time I ran the dryer. The overall electrical design and mechanical implementation is very, very poor. Would much rather have my old Kenmore dryer - lasted 30 years. During that time, I had to replace the heating element twice (once at 10 years, once at 20 years). Short product lifetime rooted in a terrible design.

Was less than a year (10 months) before I got an E63 error with this part. The problem is that the sheet metal in the center is too thin of a gauge and it warped with the continuous temperature cycling. Eventually, the coils contacted the outer housing causing the ground fault (E63).

2. If you are someone living in an apartment that does not allow washers I can assure you the packaging for this machine has the word Panda stamped on the front of the box. Unless your landlord is aware what that could mean you should have no problems.

I live in a small two-bedroom apartment in a city and was so tired of having to go to the laundromat as I had done for over four years. Enter the Panda Small Compact Portable Washing Machine. There are some great videos of other Panda washers here on Amazon. I recommend taking a look at those, particularly the one of this model's smaller size.

This little unit is fantastic. I've now used it a couple dozen times and it works great. With the spin dryer, your clothes will come out significantly drier than they would out of a washer--there will be no dripping and you can place your clothes on a rack and they'll be more or less dry in 12-24 hours in the summer (I keep mine in the bathtub and luckily have a window right there). So it's a bit more work, takes a bit more involvement, but did I mention it will save you from trips to the laundromat?

You'll want to use less soap and a little fabric softener. Your clothes won't be as soft and fluffy as they would if you used a regular dryer, but again, it's a cost and benefit analysis here: more expensive, mind-numbing trips to the laundromat or clothes that are air dried? If you have space and can afford it, perhaps the Panda dryer or something similar would be a great option, but I haven't tried it. This works just fine for my needs.

You'll also want to clean that lint catcher after washing, particularly if you have a pet. Also, I put mine in my bathroom and just put the water outlet hose in the bathtub

I may have been responsible - while the machine was washing, I kept filling it with water...and forgot all about it. When I remembered, the water had overflowed into the rinse/spinner basin which was now half full. While the washer was still washing, I switched it to drain. I heard it struggle for a second then it started to drain. I turned it off a few minutes later and that was the last time it worked.
I emailed the Amazon seller, First&Best Inc to see if it could be repaired or if there was a pump I could buy. They were incredibly gracious and friendly and accommodating. After troubleshooting the problem with me, they agreed it was the pump, and they immediately send a replacement pump over. It arrived a week later. I replaced it today and it again works like a charm! From now on I will be more gentle with it :-P
But one important thing they didn't explain, which you need to know if you have to replace the pump: You need to disassemble the pump assembly first. The hoses attached to the broken pump can not be removed. They are glued on. Remove the screws from the broken pump - you end up with 2 halves. One half has the hoses attached; the other half has the motor. Take apart the good pump in the same way. Attached the good motor to the hose assembly. Cut the old wires and splice on the new wires

Do be aware that the user guide says not to use water hotter than 115F if you use the hose supplied with the machine (120F is the maximum if you fill it with a bucket), so you can't do a 140F standard hot wash in it. The clothes do come clean even with the "hand hot" wash. The user guide also warns against overfilling the wash tub or it can leak on the floor.

The user guide fails to mention one of the most common attributes of twin-tub washers, which is you can do most or all of the rinses in the spinner: you can connect the hose to the spinner side of the machine and open the faucet while it's spinning to do a spray rinse; you can also fill the spin basket with water while it's not running and then spin. While this is not an ideal rinse and you may want to do a final rinse on the washer side once you drain the dirty water and replace it with clean water (and possibly fabric softener), it does make the cycle go faster.

If you want to, you can wash white/light clothing that is not too dirty, spin the clothes while returning the water to the washer side

Washing part is fine. The "drying" part is not good. however long you leave the clothes in the dryer, they will be damp. You'll have to hang all the clothes up and air dry them, so it's pretty much useless.

To keep the lint from adhering to my clothes and to keep it from catching in the machinery of the draining apparatus of the machine, I use an aquarium fish net to catch free floating lint.
At first, I purchased a small aquarium fish net. It wasn't big enough, so I bought the largest size.

As the load agitates, I hold the aquarium fish net against the side of the tub in the water and catch an amazingly large quantity of lint--cat hair, fabric pile, and fiber--for a 10 lb. load, sometimes up to a cup--I use the "white water" for cleaning the toilet and other household uses. I like conserving resources.

A good compact washer that I bought for a mountain cabin. I have done about 5 loads so far. The agitation is quite good, much better than I expected and almost as good as my full size machine. The spin portion of the machine does an excellent job of getting excess moisture out. As other reviewers have noted, the "fill hose" is a joke. I use mine in the bathroom and bring the shower sprayer over. The spin portion has a water input, but nothing in the manual or online addresses its use. I have put clean water into it as it is spinning, so I assume it adds a final rinse. This is not an automatic washing machine where you toss in clothes, detergent, and set a dial so you can go off and do something else waiting for the bell to ring. You are doing much of the motions: add water, drain, move to spinner, set timers for each step, etc. It is, for me, an excellent alternative to trips to the laundromat (hour and a half drive one way) and the waiting. My clothes come out clean. Yes, there is the plastic smell that others have mentioned, and we will just have to wait and see about durability.

I bought this item back in May (while still living in a house with a W/D), and used it for the first time earlier today in my new apartment.

I have it set up in my bathroom, on a folded up bath towel to cut down on any vibration and catch any minor leaks. I set up the drainage hose to empty into a 10 gallon bucket, so I could potentially reuse the wash water for a second load.

My first load was 10 T-shirts, with enough water to fill it to the M line (~8 gallons of warm water; filled by hand with a small bucket from the bathtub faucet, plus 1 T laundry detergent). The wash cycle seemed to work fine. Drainage was a bit of a problem, because I discovered that to fully drain the unit, the unit should ideally be a few inches above the end of the drainage hose. Although I could drain about 3/4 of the water into my 10 gallon bucket, the last bit required draining into a shallow bowl (repeatedly dumping and then letting more water drain). This was slightly annoying.

After the wash and drain, when I attempted the rinse cycle, nothing happened. I discovered that I'd blown the circuit breaker on the outlet. Not sure why that happened (it didn't happen for my second load), but after re-setting it I kept a closer eye on it.

The rinse water I drained into the bathtub (still needed the shallow pan to remove the last bit of it). The water still seemed a little grungy, so it made me wonder how clean, or well-rinsed, the clothes really were.

We've washed about a dozen loads in this, so far, and have been very happy with it. We watched a few videos on this machine prior to ordering it, so we knew to expect a little extra work on our part compared to a standard washing machine. The hose fits our kitchen sink without issue, but we also fill the tub with buckets of water. We fill two buckets and set them aside, then hook up the hose to the kitchen faucet and begin filling the tub. While the faucet is filling the tub, we pour in the buckets of water, add detergent and our clothing and wait for the faucet to finish filling the tub to the correct water level. While the clothes are washing/agitating, we fill the buckets again to prepare for the rinse cycle. This saves time on the overall process.
As other reviewers have said, clothes do get twisted. I try to gently untangle them at various stages of the process - usually while the tub is draining/filling. This way clothes don't get too twisted. It hasn't been a big deal for us.
We've been very pleased with our little washer and hope it lasts!

Was a bit nervous when purchasing this, as some reviewers complained of leaking and other problems, but I'm very satisfied! It's the perfect size for my tiny apartment and washes the perfect amount of clothes per load. I was actually pleasantly surprised by how dry the spinner gets the clothes. Unless it's heavy material like jeans or thick blankets, most items come out very lightly damp.
I think some people can be quite rough with the machine, so it's important to remember that--to give the machine a long life span--you shouldn't overload it, or run more than a couple loads at a time. Only use one side at at time too. Just try to treat it well and it'll work out fine. I've had mine for several months and the only thing I could possibly complain about it that the filling hose attachment got a bit loose on the the faucet end, but that was easily fixed by placing a small rubber band around it. This is life-changing for apartment dwellers who have to schlep up and down stairs to the basement laundry room. I had my first load in it within minutes of unpacking it. It's very easy to use, and it holds a load about half the size of a regular washer. It did a flannel king-sized sheet and a few pillow cases with no problem. Another load was 5 normal weight towels. Another was 2 pairs of chinos and 4 yoga pants. You put in your clothes, fill it with water and add detergent and set the wash cycle; come back and drain; refill and run again to rinse and drain; transfer to the spin side, and in 5 minutes they come out drier any regular washer I have used. I also purchased a Panda dryer, and my sheets and towels dried in 30 minutes or less. With coin-operated machines costing about $10 a week, I'll be saving money after 11 months.

This Panda xpb45 replaced a 3.6 cubic foot American made top-loader that cracked the outer tub during repetitive power failures and started leaking. The machine was only 4 1/2 years old. The Panda has surprised us by creating really dirty, opaque, wash water on the first loads we ran. I thought at first that it was really dirty clothes, but when I washed a load of unworn "clean" shirts from the closet, the wash water was still grey and dirty looking. After 3 or 4 times through the wash cycle without changing detergents or spot treatments the wash water looks like one would expect, a little dirty (brownish), but not opaque.

The Panda lets me soak a load overnight if necessary or convenient. Its' predecessor would automatically drain after 3 or 4 hours in a soak cycle unless it was unplugged from the wall. I used to pretreat even small bloodstains with hydrogen peroxide to remove them. With the new machine, unless it is a large bloodstain, it washes out without pre-treatment.

Washing is now a manual process which requires minor thought. I actually have to remember whether it just finished a wash cycle or a soak cycle. The spin-rinse tub works surprisingly well, I always liked the spin-rinses that the washers of the 60's had. I know it is not intended, but a spin-rinse on clothes with hanger dust on them is usually enough to run them through dryer and wear them. We may save enough money from the shorter time that the electric dryer runs

I love my Panda! This is a semi-automatic washing machine that requires your supervision to complete laundry. I have a Bosch Nexxt 500 series that needed several new parts and I had laundry backing up because the parts were on back order. That machine has since been repaired and is working well once more. I have learned a lot about washing in my Panda.
First of all do not place your Panda in a bathtub to do laundry. There are air intake areas that will cause the machine to malfunction if water is drawn into the motor area. Do not raise the drain hose higher than the tub of the machine. With my setup I can drain it directly into my commode and it pumps fine. It needs about a 1/2 teaspoon of liquid HE detergent to clean very well. Do not allow your control timers to get wet as this may cause machine to not work. I keep two hand towels and mop up water on the edges of the tub when I transfer my laundry to the spinner. I only fill the spinner 3/4 full and only set it to 2 1/2 minutes for the most wet items. Place your heaviest item in the spinner first. If it is a bulky item such as jeans or a corduroy shirt I only spin that item. You can tell if you need an additional minute of spin time if you are still having water flow from the drain hose when it stops you need a little extra spin. When I opened mine, all the chains had gotten tangled up so it took a good 5-7 minutes to untangle everything. Once that was accomplished, I set to making the tea. Here are the pros and cons:

Pros:

Easy to use

the latch works well and actually holds (unlike a lot of the other ones)
the little clip that holds the whole thing together is of good quality and hasn't broken (my experience has been that the clip is the most important part. They fall apart after a day or two of use and so tea ball won't stay closed which makes the whole thing useless)....yet.

Cons:

For my use, the tea balls are too small. I brew an enormous pot everyday and so I have to use 3 of these tea balls. I put roses in one and the tea in the other two. That makes a pot big enough for 8-12 cups.

But overall, I like these a lot and I think it's a good product.

I received a sample for review.

The Friendly Swede's stainless steel mesh tea balls, come in a set of six, and are capable of holding enough loose tea leaves, to make several servings of tea. These balls perform this task very well, and have a chain with a hook, for removing it from your cup or small kettle when the tea is ready.

For the most part, these balls are pretty nicely made. A latch securely holds the two halves of the ball in place, and the fit of the covers is nice and tight. Only tiny particles can slip through the mesh, so hopefully your tea won't have much sediment. The only negative I found was that the metal hinge on some of the balls, had a sharp edge that needed to be smoothed out. Stainless steel is easier to keep clean and resists stains, but proper cleaning is still required to prevent the buildup of any residual matter.

People like their tea at different strengths, and a set of these balls allows each person to control how much flavor they want. Well made, and easy to use, these balls could make an attractive addition to your tea service. With a diameter of about 1.5" a single ball probably does not hold enough tea to make a large potfull, but if you use two or three balls, you can probably accomplish this task.

Details.
Purchased for Maytag Dryer MEDX500XW0 (switch used on many makes and models). I accidentally broke the original switch while replacing the dryer's rollers and drive belt. The OEM switch is only glued together and a hard yank on the wires pulled it apart. Prime is addictive. I was willing to wait two days to save ten dollars when compared with local price.
The OEM unit has three studs in one half with matching holes in the other. In the OEM unit the studs are only used to keep the two halves in alignment. The switch is held together with urethane glue. On the purchased unit no glue is used. Instead, the three stud ends are melted with a soldering iron to hold the two halves together. (see photo). It might not make any difference but one starts to question where and how this switch is put together.

There are so many of these pumps on Amazon that it is difficult to know which is OEM, authentic, or otherwise. I paid $29 for a pump from A+ Supply, and the description explicitly says that it is an authentic LG part. I can confirm that it is. My pump came in a brown package with a label and bar code for an "LG #XXXXXXX". Don't be put off by the box--it is a "track pack" intended for service professionals rather than consumers. (Consumer packs would have pictures, descriptions, and instructions.) Moreover, the part itself has "PLASET" molded in--that is the Italian manufacturer, and it matches the mold marks on the the old pump and the recirculation pump. It slid in perfectly, and everything lined up with no hitches. Once I got it back together, the washer is as good as new.

If your LG washer displays the OE error, that indicates a pump failure; my original pump failed when the impeller cracked and was rattling around inside the bell housing. If you get that error and it has a loud sound, it is probably a similar issue. Rather than taking the entire machine apart, tip it up and back. I was able to replace the pump by coming up through the open bottom of the machine. It was a bit tight, but very doable.

It requires a special spreader tool to expand it far enough to slip on. Since I didn't have one I improvised and asked for help. It took three hands and three flat head screwdrivers to pry it back on. Just put the ring on as far as you can by hand and then slowly wedge the ring down. Easy peasy. The first one of these I purchased, a couple of years ago, was a perfect replacement and is pleasantly in service. Another, identical, fan in my home started rattling, so I ordered another one of these, and, it was not a perfect replacement.

First, the fan itself, I think the only the plastic part, is a bit warped. This will shorten the life (torquing it during spinning, causing hte bearings to wear faster).

Second, the body is not a perfect fit. The flat portion is a several mms off spec, being too small, and the folded sides of the metal were both a bit longer and the tabs, a bit bigger. The end result was that, as is, the fan does not lock in place on insertion, instead, being too small, it will just fall out. I bent the folded sides outward, and squished the tabs down to make them thinner and that worked. Overall, a job that should have been 5 minutes took 20, and a fan that should last 10-20 years will probably last 5-10. That said, I don't know of an alternative :(

An easy fix! After about 7 years, our Samsung Dryer belt was falling apart. Thanks to the internet, there is a video to show how to take apart and install the new belt. My dryer is the gas version. You do not even have to unhook the gas (or the vent tubing) to change the belt! Unplug the dryer, take the top off and follow the instructions to take the pieces off of the front.

Watch the video to see how the belt wraps around the idler pulley. There are a few possible ways to install it, and only 1 right way so that the belt grooves are on the right side at the motor. You have to do this by feel when you leave the dryer in place. If you can get to the back, removing the access cover WILL make routing the belt around the pulley easier...but it isn't required. It's the front of the dryer that needs to be disassembled to actually change the belt.

One caveat: Be sure you pick up any pieces of the old belt that you find floating around loose. You don't want them getting picked up and knocking the new belt off of the tensioner pulley.

I am an Amazon seller, and send my products to their distribution centers for order fulfillment. This is a great sealer for sealing my products (mostly apparel), to keep the dust out. Currently I am using 2 mil bags, which are pretty durable, and you can also use poly tubing. The 16" width is long in comparison to others, but we sell corsets, dresses and other items which require a wider, 15" bag. It works just as well when sealing smaller width bags.

The sealer itself is pretty easy to use. I like the all-metal housing of this brand, versus the cheap plastic housing some others brands have. Because it has a metal housing, it has some "heft", and will not bounce around when quickly using it when sealing, and won't go flying across the table if you bump it. Overall, a nice product and a decent value.

Note: This will hermetically seal the bag completely, making it airtight. If you are selling apparel or similar items that might have a risk of damage from moisture, you might want to add a dessicant (i.e. a silica gel pack), to help absorb any moisture, if you are packing and sealing products in a humid environment. I use 1-gram silica gel packs, and you can find them on Amazon. The alternative is to punch a small hole in the corner of the sealed bag, so the item can "breathe," but then you risk warehouse dust making its way in.

This sealer is easy to use and fairly light weight. It comes with an extra heating element wire and heat resistant cloth. After experimenting with the heat dial, I found just below the half point is good for quick sealing of 75 gauge CF polyolefin shrink film.

This is the real McCoy of reviews. I know this product front-to-back, it's positives and shortcomings. I used to work at an industrial aircraft part warehouse, and this product, in various lengths, was THE sealer we used. So I've operated this and the other length options THOUSANDS of times.
This is how it works: there's a piece of teflon tape on the bottom covering a wire heating element/filament. This flat wire is removable, as is the teflon strip, making replacement easy, which is good, as both do not last forever (think of a lightbulb filament, only one with much more electricity passing through it, and the teflon tape is only teflon-coated paper, which will burn and crack after a number of uses, possibly 100, depending on the heat level and care it is treated with). The heat is controlled by a dial knob. The element heats up when the upper bar is pulled down, which compresses the two plastic sheets. The thicker the sheets, the longer you need the bar down and the higher you need the heat. Again, the filament is on the bottom, and both sheet's need to be melted enough to adhere, so plan the heat level accordingly. I've sealed thin, sandwich bag-thick bags, bubble wrap, potato chip bags, as well as thick industrial strength vinyl bags.
The sealer's casing is of strong metal design, industrial, and durable to a moderate amount of disgruntled employee abuse (heh).

Day 1 Review: Overall Pretty Good, Purchased it for my lab down here in El Paso because it gets hot a bullocks over here and it make really good ice after throwing out the first 5 batches. Ice is pretty uniform and good for chewing, I love chewing ice so this was a big deal for me, but has a pretty small specific heat capacity (1 ice cube of X area will cool your drink a smaller amount compared to other ice), but hey it was a pretty cheap solution for my problem. I am taking off one star because there are 2 glaring issues. Issue 1 is there should be a storage area outside the container to hold to scoop. Right now it is currently taking up valuable basket space for my ice. Nothing a trip to the local hardware store or 3d printing lab across the hall and some glue cant fix but still shouldnt need to do more work to manage the accessories. The second and more glaring problem is that the ice has a small and large function, which I thought would produce different diameter ice, It does not. the ice is made with a cylindrical hole in the middle and changing large to small will only increase the diameter of this hole but not the diamater of the cube itself. this leads to some less than optimal packing factors for the limited space of ice storage. Overall dont regret the purchase and it was resonably priced in comparison with other products, Would be 5 star if 20 bucks off.

So all the reviews I read about this machine were accurate. You need to put a little work into it for it to be just perfect.
What you will need:
Garden Hose
Hose connecting Adapter
Clamp Rings
Eye Hoods
Craft Wire

Working with what you have:
The hose is 2 small and you need an adapter. I found a simple solution by going to home depot and getting a clear hose to attach to the hose. Before inserting the hose I inserted a plastic connector into the open end of the washing machine hose.
This allowed the hose to remain in place in the clear hose.
I then used clamp rings to make sure it would not come out and hold it together.
I have made this portable mini washing machine into a non-movable one by putting the hose to drain in the sink.
I attached eye hooks to the wall and used craft wire to wrap around the hose and threaded it through the hooks.
The hose for intake is also too small.
Easy fix for that situation as well.
I took a garden hose found an adapter for my kitchen sink ( don't drink tap water anyway so removed tap filter to place adapter)
Now when I want to use the machine I only have to connect the hose and fill the tub with hot or cold water depending on what I'm washing.

Prior to this, I had the Panda XPB45 larger model, it's almost the same size as this Della. I had the Panda for 4 years, and it worked really well, except with time, all the electrical connectors starting failing, so I had to turn the dials several times before it would "take". Eventually, one of the dials failed completely, so it had to be discarded. I've bought this Della to replace it.

I've taken a close look, and it seems pretty much the same design as the Panda, with few differences. So far, I've only used it a handful of times, and I like it overall. The agitation is strong, and it's quite capacious. So far so good. The one DEFINITE negative compared to the Panda is that the pump is SUPER WEAK. It struggles to pump out the water, with barely a trickle, and most of the time it takes about a minute before it manages to work up any water at all. For all intents and purposes it's almost like a gravity outflow.

Now, I have the drain hose outlet about the height of the top of the machine, so it would probably do better if it was lower, but then I had the Panda at the same height, and the pump worked just fine.

The real test will be how long this machine lasts - my Panda lasted a solid 4 years, and I'd be happy if this Della did so too, but that remains to be seen.

They are a great option for specific uses such as in a tiny home or an RV, or maybe if you are renting a house without a dishwasher and can't install a full-size model. All I had to do is use the hose kit that comes with the dishwasher, cut off the part that connects to the faucet and plug that directly into the part I bought at home depot. It was snug enough I probably didn't need the hose clamp, but added it for good measure.

These filters are a good value and replace an LG refrigerator water filter LT1000P.

Once you actually get them installed - they work great and the resulting water tastes great as well.

My biggest beef with these are that they do not install easily.

When I replace a water filter in my refrigerator - I don't expect to struggle with what should be a simple task.

For this filter, both removal of the previous filter AND installation of the new filter are unnecessarily difficult.

Whether this is the fault of the filters or my LG fridge is not 100% clear, but I don't recall struggling as much with my original LG filter.

Basically, removing it is a slight pain - you have to twist counter-clockwise - very hard. It almost feels like you're going to break the fridge connection.

Installing the new one is even more difficult. Sounds crazy, but it's true. You have to really use quite a bit of force to screw it in clockwise until it locks in place - again, it feels like you're going to break the damn fridge.

Once that is accomplished however, these filters truly shine. There are no water leaks, and as I mentioned earlier, the water tastes fantastic.

So - do I recommend them? Yes. However, maybe I'm naive, but I feel like removing and installing should be as simple as a slight pull/push and a twist.

I grind my own coffee so it is important to note a couple things. The screen on the included basket will stop the majority of the silt from getting to your cup but it cannot stop everything. The best way to prevent this is to use a paper filter to keep the coffee dust in the basket and out of your coffee cup. It is also important to be careful how fine a grind you use as coffee ground too fine will clog the screen and/or the paper filter.

Slightly off topic: If you are planning to get a coffee grinder so you have total control when and how your coffee is ground, get a conical grinder so your grind is consistent. The "twirling blades of death" style of grinder really doesn't provide the proper grind consistency.

1) Ignore 'all' the instructions (the kit content, unit descriptions and color identification) that comes with the kit.
2) The kit comes with a cycling thermostat (larger unit) and 2 thermal fuses:
a) Electric dryer - Use the one rated to 150 Degrees Celsius. Approx. 302 Degrees Fahrenheit
b) Gas dryer - User the one rated to 115 Degrees Celsius. Approx. 239 Degrees Fahrenheit
3) FYI, once a fuse is blown (if the unit gets too hot) you have to replace it. Fuses only work once.
4) You should replace both the cycling thermostat and the thermal fuse since most of the time the reason for
which a thermal fuse is blown is because the cycling thermostat is faulty (... and you get both in the kit
anyways).

As you can see from the picture, the K-Cup Holder Assembly (left) and the "Old" version of the My K-Cup (center) are nearly an inch longer than the New version of the My K-Cup (right). So it is time to update this review. First about me: My wife and I have 4 kids with the youngest in diapers (we also use cloth diapers). So that being said, our washer and dryer are well used (at least one load a day if not more). We have a Kenmore Elite HE3t that we bought new from Sears in 2002. The only thing that has really gone wrong has been this pump. The original one lasted until November 2018. So that is when I bought my first replacement pump, this one right here that I am reviewing. When I bought it, it had a LIFETIME guarantee. Yes, a Lifetime guarantee on it. What can be better than a relatively inexpensive part (more than they are now) and a lifetime guarantee? I thought sold. Even if it breaks in a few years I can get a new one for free.

Well, it didn't make it a few years. It didn't even make a it a year. It broke in October of 2019, less than 11 months from when I installed it. But remember, it had a lifetime guarantee. So I contacted the manufacturer and they asked for some pictures and then had me order another one from Amazon. They then credited me through Amazon for the replacement. I thought that was pretty nice and that maybe I got a bad part since it broke in less than 11 months. So where did it break? It broke on the impeller. It cracked on the hub and came apart from the back piece. The motor also had water in it as I am assuming that is due to the seal failing when the impeller and hub came apart.

The product arrived on time, was heavier than the original pump motor which was nice. It fit in well and was an easy install. I liked that it came with a spare o-ring in case I ever need to remove it for any reason. Had no problems pumping water through an extended drain hose.

FYI. I ordered this Dryer Door Switch "blind" (I did NOT open the dryer hood BEFORE I placed the order through Amazon. So when the new switch got here and I popped the hood of my dryer (following a YouTube "How To" video for my Kenmore dryer), I noticed that the switches WERE IDENTICAL, but the Part #'s were off by the last 3~4 digits... I tried it anyway since I got it and it WORKED. As soon as I plugged the 240v plug back into its receptacle the dryer light illuminated! 😉😁
Keep in mind I ordered this particular one over others because of the SLIGHTLY longer wires between the plug and the switch, not to mention the wire "tie" that came pre-installed to keep the wire aaay from the rotation of the drum. Switch worked flawlessly right from the start! 😎

⚠️ ⚠️ Lastly, I would caution you on the plug side and make sure you are careful removing the old switch from the plug because there are two (one on each side of plug) locking teeth that keeps the plug from vibrating loose. Also, depending on the type of plastic the plug is made out of it may be brittle do to the heat of the dryer.

Hope this helps.

The metal shaft, the most critical part of the part was poorly machined. The first crusher blade that I slid onto the shaft fit perfectly until it got about 3/8 inch from the end of the flat part of the shaft and wouldn't go any farther. So I had to dig out the Dremel tool then go buy a small grinding stone so I could re-machine the last 3/8 inch of the flat part of the shaft. This meant grinding a small amount on one side of the shaft and trying the blade. Then grinding the other side of the shaft and trying the blade. Doing this until the blade would slide all the way down the shaft but still be a snug fit so the center hole of the crusher blade didn't get distorted by a loose shaft in that area.
This turned a 30 minute repair job into over half a day.
How does BlueStar machine a shaft perfectly except for 3/8 inch from the end of the flattened sides of the shaft? That's just por quality control.
BlueStar needs to look into the manufacturing of this part. Evidently this is a recent issue because the only other review that mentions this problem was the one Angel did on Dec. 21, 2018. Broke the blades on mine when the ice maker quit and I started freezing ice cube tray ice and dumping it in the ice bin. Don't Do This! Ice tray, store ice is Larger than the cubes from the ice maker - they will jam and break the plastic screw blades. Finally did what I should have - took ice maker apart, fixed the ice rotator dispenser, replaced the auger, and, ice again.
CAVEAT: Pay VERY close attention to the ice chopping blades on the front of the auger you are replacing. Do Not remove them until You Are Sure you know the Exact order how to put them back on the new auger. THESE BLADES AND SPACERS GO ON IN A SPECIFIC ORDER AND THE BLADES IN A SPECIFIC ROTATION DIRECTION. I did not and spent a few wasted hours searching the internet before I got them back on the right way. And, be careful, there are small metal washesr between the spacers and are easy to drop and spend a long time finding them.

Even though the Amazon ad says this is an exact fit for a WR 17x1139 auger, it really wasn't. The threaded shaft with a flat flange to hold the metal retaining washers was about a quarter inch shorter than the original part from my refrigerator. Several reviews recommended grinding the shaft to make it about a quarter of an inch longer for holding the 2 fixed blades, 3 rotating blades and the original number of nylon washers. That is completely unnecessary. Since this auger replaces so many different models, not all were an EXACT fit, but it can easily be made to fit and work without grinding the shaft. It turns out that the thickness of one flat nylon washer is exactly the same thickness as the length of the shaft to the flat flange is short. By eliminating 1 flat nylon washer, the Auger can be made to work perfectly. Another important point to pay attention to is that the 3 rotating blades have a single digit number stamped into each of them. Mine were 7, 8 & 9. It is important to keep these in numerical order so that they progressively and evenly advance to crush the ice.

I wish I had taken a picture of my final configuration, but the sequence of blades and washers went like this:
1. Two metal Slotted washers against the flange
2. Rotating blade #7 with the numbered side down toward the metal washers
3. Dual diameter nylon washer with the larger diameter portion against blade 7 & the smaller diameter being inserted into the first statio

As others have stated, this is a bare bones ice maker replacement. No wiring harness. No clips. I transferred my double wire hanger from my original Amana ice maker to this one, to ensure ice maker shuts off when the bin is full. The single wire hanger doesn't raise high enough as the ice bin fills to activate the shut-off mechanism. I added a picture of the double wire hanger.
The piece for the water fill tube indicates the area where a "tab" should be removed to allow for the tube, but that tab doesn't just snap out, though it looks like it should. You have to cut it out with a knife, or some other tool (I used a Dremel), though it probably would have been easier to use the original piece from my old unit.
You may need to "prime" the ice maker after installation. This can be done by removing the front white cover and inserting a small INSULATED jumper cable into the holes identified with "T" and "H". You can find instructions on how to do this safely on YouTube (Search "Testing Ice Maker").
I kept most of the items from my old unit in case anything fails or breaks on this new one in the future, such as the thermostat, sweeper arms, and tray (for the heater element).

I got one of those 4 item dryer replacement kits from Amazon, but the cycling thermostat said 240 volts, which I assume is for the heater element (2 smaller pins) since all electric dryers use 240 volts.  I bought this one because it said 120 volts, and the thermostat heater in my dryer runs off a 120 volt circuit, and is supposed to have a resistance of ~ 3500 ohms.  This one had a resistance of 7800 ohms, the same as the 240 volt version.  After changing out the faulty 250F high limit therm from the original order and replacing the 309F fuse in that kit with a 352F fuse (per spec), the dryer works and cycles OK now, but I am keeping it on the delicate setting for now since I don't want it to get too hot and blow out the high limit (352F) fuse again.  Even the delicate setting gets plenty hot, but I wish all these dryer parts had better specs listed so you wouldn't have to order over and over again to find the right combination.  But they are all made in China so it's hard to tell what you're going to get.

When they are tapped in place I recommend a 9/16 socket placed on the metal hub, tap lightly with a hammer until seated this shears off the nubs inside the bore which are there to provide the tight fit. Our Kenmore 80 series dryer would continue to run despite the door being open, causing clothes to tumble out.

Lifted the dryer lid to find that I could probably just replace this harness. Looked the part up on amazon to find this wonderful replacement.

If you open the dryer door and look at the switch itself, two Phillips screws hold the switch assembly in place. I removed them and disconnected the switch’s wire harness.

I was too lazy to grab a flathead or another tool, so I used a knife to act as a flathead to free the switch’s wire harness from where it connects to the rest of the dryer’s harness.

Popped the new assembly into place, screwed the two Phillips head screws in, and connected the wire harnesses.

Total time for job: 60 seconds
Tools used: Phillips screwdriver and flathead (or similar tool)

From the Manufacturer:
[Portable design, outsized production] The NewAir countertop ice Maker takes up only about one square foot of counter space, but don't let its size fool you. This compact ice maker makes 33 pounds of ice each day — and looks great doing it. That’s almost the same as purchasing three 10lb bags of store-bought ice in a single day. Choose from three Great colors to match your decor.
[Fast freezing means more ice] need ice quick? The NewAir countertop ice Maker makes a new batch of ice every eight minutes. Use the included scoop and removable ice tray to empty it regularly, and you'll have enough ice for any occasion

I have mixed feelings about this machine. My first beef is with the advertising. The manufactures states "The NewAir countertop ice Maker produces 33 pounds of bullet ice each day, so you'll never run out". While this may be true, it's not at all realistic. You would have to stand near the machine all day and add water and empty out the ice. The bin is quite small and is not a freezer so the ice will melt in short order. It does make a batch of ice in less than 10 minutes, however a batch is about one serving. I'm trying to figure out how this will be useful, but it's just not practical. If you need large amounts of ice for an event, you will be better off purchasing ice and storing it in a cooler. If you need small amounts of ice, I suspect your ice maker could keep up and if you don't have an automatic ice maker in your freeze you could buy plastic ice cube trays for a lot less money. This leaves it for use in a campsite, RV or boat. Again, I think it requires too much attention to be useful and takes up too much space in any of those settings. As far as the unit itself, it's about the footprint of a 6 slice toaster. It makes a batch (small) in less than 10 minutes. About a glass full. The bin holds enough ice for about 4 glasses but is not refrigerated. So in summary, it does make small amounts of ice rather quickly and it's not terribly expensive. However, I think this a novelty item that will wind up as a yard sale item in short order.

PERFECT appliance for this use! Basically plug ‘n play after washing the parts that water/ice will touch.
The bullet cubes are excellent - my husband is a vodka on the rocks guy, so ice kinda matters. These have zero smell or taste & melt evenly.
You fill the reservoir with water & 8 mins later, your 1st “batch” of cubes drop. Enough for 1 rocks glass full. They keep making until the bin is full & indicator lights tell you when it’s full or out of water.

We’ve been turning this off when we’re done using it, then back on shortly before needing it again, but if this were for all day use, you’d need to keep an eye on it. If all the ice is made & you don’t use them, they melt back in & make cubes again! Sometimes the cubes stack up to the top & triggers the “ice full” light, so just spreading them out turns the light off & it continues making ice.

There’s supposedly 2 sizes of bullet cubes, but we see no discernible difference. Haven’t put a ruler to ‘em, but they look pretty much the same! No big deal to us - the large is small enough!
The whole thing is about the size of a large air fryer or an old school bread

HOLY c- these are a godsend. I unknowingly bought a new ge stainless steel electric range with the sensi temp coils which everyone hates and now I see why. GE legally says they cant be replaced with regular but its just liability/legal jargon. They can indeed be replaced with this. I went to homedepot before going here and 1 small size element was $29 and the larger was $35 at the time for the regular GE elements without sensitemp. The fact this is a fullset of 4 for the price of basically 1.5 of the regular ones, its worth it.

Now theres a small downside which isnt a deal breaker. The Y bracket the coil sits on doesnt have all coils clipped onto it, the coils are somewhat floating over it and only held onto by the end ring but its not a problem when something is on it. The other thing is my larger element was not centered. Like i fit it in and the base fit perfectly but the coil rings were off to the left. Still works as it should but have to align pans to the coil location and not presume middle of the under drip pan is where the middle of the coil is.

That being said Im free of sensi temp elements and can finally boil water without the stove shutting itself off. Thanks GE for being lazy and not integrating sensitemp into the actual unit with digital signals but just modded the elements of the stove making it completely backwards compatible with these elements.

The overall performance of the EFP Humidifier Filters (wicks) replacement for HDC12 AIRCARE filters (wicks) is affected by one difference. The Aircare HDC12 wick is made with the pass-through of outside air going straight through the wick in see-through channels which picks up the moisture from the wick and carries humid air into my home effectively. The EFP wick has layers that are overlaying one another causing some of the airflow to be restricted resulting for less humidity to be released in the same amount of time.

I found that the water in the Aircare HD1409 humidifier using the HDC12 wick was taking up the water in humidifier containers in about 18 hours requiring them to be refilled. The EFP wick used up about half the water in the same time.

In the dry climate we have in the winter time in Eastern Colorado, we want the humidifier to put out as much moisture as possible. The humidifier has auto sensing to selected humidity and auto-turnoff so getting the right humidity level is not difficult. The EPF wick didn't release enough moisture for the humidifier to turn off once settings were reached. I have family members that live in Oregon that use a similar humidifier but, because the outside humidity is higher, they can use the EPF wick with no problem.

These humidifier filters are definitely low cost.  However the real purpose of these filters is not to filter the air but to wick water from the reservoir to be able to evaporate and add moisture to your house.  For that purpose they work well.

I’ve had these installed for a week or so now. Noticed that the humidifier was going through less water than with very old oem wicks. RH of the garage is also lower. So I touched the wick and it’s mostly dry. Tbf I run these at high speed 24/7 which was never an issue. Idk it’s possible these may work if you’re using this intentionally oversized to keep noise down but these don’t keep up with what the machine is capable of.

I put everything on ice and started looking at the freezer. Both the power light and run light were on but the compressor was not running.

I pulled the compressor start relay and tested it. It was defective.

I called Curtis International's customer service, who manufactures the freezer for Igloo. I gave them all the information about the freezer and asked for a transfer to the parts department or a technician. I was informed that they do not transfer calls, but another department would email me. Three days later, I received an email asking for exactly the same information I gave over the phone.

I provided all the information along with a picture of the broken part. I was informed that because the freezer was beyond the one year warranty, Curtis International would provide no support. They suggested I call a local repair person.

For anyone who has a similar problem, the compressor start relay is part number qp2-4.7g12. You can find it on many part supply websites.

First of all I did not buy one of these from Amazon but obtained one from someone who did. Theirs failed after 2 years, they tried to fix it and failed, and then gave it to me.. Reading these reviews I am seeing many of the same complaints.

After troubleshooting I found the Motor Starting Relay bad. Part number is QP2-4.7. You can buy them cheaply from Amazon. Or you can remove the Motor Starting Relay, Start Capacitor, and Motor Overload Switch and replace them with a Supco 3 n 1 Hard Start Kit for $12 and this will have a lot more reliability.

They are inexpensive and nice freezers however if you buy one you need to also buy a spare motor starting relay or a Supco 3 n 1 (RCO810) because this relay will fail in a year or two. I've seen it a lot of times and I'm reading about it here.

Anyone can change the relay in just a few minutes. It isn't hard. But mark my words. If you buy this freezer (also branded under IGLOO, CURTIS, THOMPSON, etc.) you need to also buy the starting relay for a spare.

This kit includes a heater, thermister and thermostat supposedly to repair a GE Refrigerator among others.  I've experimented carefully with all 3 items received in this kit.  Heater:  Works fine, had it for about 6 months now.  Thermister: Not in spec.  The correct OHM reading should be 16 OHM at 32 deg F for a GE fridge.  The one in this kit measured 24 OHM at 32 deg F.  This will not work, it causes fridge to think it's much colder than it really is causing the fridge temp to be way to warm.  Thermostat: Garbage.  It's supposed to open up at about 40 deg F and above (i.e. create open circuit).  The one in this kit stays closed all the time.  I connected a meter to it and soaked it in hot water (about 80 + deg F) for 10 minutes and it never opened up.  This is dangerous because the thermostat is supposed to prevent the heater from overheating the freezer compartment.  I'm not sure if I happen to receive defective parts or if they are all defective.  Either way, 2 out of 3 bad parts is not a good sign.

This was a good replacement for the defrost heater. My old one might actually have been OK because I found when replacing that the wire spade connections were corroded with surface rust from the wet environment, so I added high temp dielectric grease to protect going forward. But it works well.

The thermistor was WAY OFF CALIBRATION. You need to really really make sure that at 32F (ice water) the resistance is 16.3K. What I got in this product read 35K... since the thermistor determines when the defrost heater shuts off, the result was my defrost cycle would take the freezer compartment to 70F+, melting everything. Also, the thermistor needs to be mounted on the topmost pipe of the evaporator... top topmost. Lower (like where the thermostat is) results in reading too cold and again, overheating by a little.

The thermostat is really just an overtemp protection to shut off at 140F, in normal operation it does nothing. The unit provided in this kit is OK but has a less secure latching clip than the OEM part, which makes it more likely to fall off the evap pipe.

This heater is essentially a "moving" part (it heats and cools by a wide range), and will go bad at some point. This replacement does not seem to have the longevity of the OEM heater given it's somewhat different materials (mine died in 9 months vs 7 years for the OEM). Consider a pricier real OEM part given that the heater operates in pretty hostile conditions, and will do about 0.5-3 defrost cycles per 24 hours.

But do not fear - the customer service for this particular offering is excellent. Don't hesitate to contact them in case you want a refund for this one so that you can buy the genuine one. I got a prompt refund upon request.

A pro tip here - if you are replacing the heater, just defrost the heater bracket itself, and install the new heater. Then turn on the fridge, enter the diagnostics mode by pushing the 4 temperature adjustment buttons at once (getting to the blinking 00 00 on the temperature panel), and toggle "1 4" mode to turn on the heater. The heater will light up. Wait for it to work and defrost the rest of the coil. To turn the heater off when done, toggle "1 4" mode again. Please see the attached images on how this works in practice. You also get an extra bonus, you get to see your new heater in action!

If something bubbles over on the stove, the liquid will definitely get underneath these covers and make a mess. They're also not entirely flame resistant. I have different sized burners on my stove, and sometimes the one specifically trimmed for each burner doesn't make it back to the right spot. After 2 years of use, most of them have burned edges and have become too brittle to use anymore. 1. The information on Amazon for this Tier 1 RWF1021 replacement filter did not indicate the contaminants it is rated for reducing. The carton for the original Kenmore 9915 filter says it reduces chlorine, particulate Class I, lead, mercury, benzene, p-Dichlorobenzene, asbestos and cysts. According to the information printed on the Tier 1 filter, it says "independently tested against ANSI/NSF 42 Standards, for reduction of chlorine taste and odor." According to the NSF website, ANSI/NSF 42 establishes minumum requirements for "reduction of aesthetic or non-health-related contaminants (chlorine, taste, odor and particulates) that may be present in public or private drinking water." That evidently means the Tier 1 only filters chlorine and particulates. Therefore it is not an exact replacement for the Kenmore 9915. However, it is all I need for my purposes, because my tap water is perfectly healthy. It just tastes better without the chlorine.

2. The rectangular piece on the end of the filter that fits into a slot on the cap in my refrigerator is a tiny bit narrower than the original 9915. This means it fits more loosely into the slot. However, it still works well enough to be usable in my refrigerator.

All things considered - including the much lower than original 9915 price - I will probably order this filter again.

Would give a five, but...there must be a change in whoever manufactured this part. We had ordered this same part a few years ago and it fit exactly onto the shaft it needs to go on. However, with this one, it doesn’t slid on at all. There’s a 1000th of an inch difference (or less) in the Inner Diameter (ID) of the bushing from the previous part to this one.

Here’s how I fixed it. Take a half inch drill (fits perfectly) bit and run it on the inside of the part for about a minute or two while rotating the part at the same time. This ensures the ID is rounded out as evenly as possible. You will notice the smallest amount of metal powder appearing on the part and in your hand. Check the fit of the pulley onto the shaft. You may have to repeat this process a few times until the pulley fits perfectly onto the shaft AND spins freely as it should.
